research.summary: Team logos and athlete headshots sit on very different legal footing for a small betting-adjacent media app. Logos: nominative fair use protects using a team NAME to identify a game, but the Ninth Circuit line of cases (New Kids, Volkswagenwerk, Toyota v. Tabari) treats a stylized logo as "more of the mark than necessary" when the word mark would do, logos can also carry copyright, and Apple App Review does not accept fair-use arguments at all: it asks for rights documentation on letterhead or removal (documented rejections under 5.2.1 / 4.1 for NBA, FIFA and European club logos). League licensing (NFL Properties, NBA Properties, CLC) is built for merchandise with minimum guarantees and years-in-business screens; no public small-app digital logo program was found. ESPN CDN logo/headshot URLs are governed by Disney's terms (personal, noncommercial, no scraping, no "building a business"), so they are not licensed for third-party use. Commercial image vendors (Sportradar, SportsDataIO, Stats Perform) either exclude betting use outright or expressly disclaim any league logo license; every sports API surveyed (Sportmonks, API-Football, TheSportsDB, SportsDataIO's WikipediaLogoUrl) says the logos are not licensed and the customer must secure rights. Headshots: editorial photo licensing exists (Getty Editorial $167/mo for 10 downloads, AP metered) but is editorial-only and per-image; Wikimedia Commons CC photos are free to use commercially with attribution (what tennis_photos.js already does), with the caveat that CC covers copyright only, not personality rights, though California's 3344(d) sports-account exemption and Gionfriddo/C.B.C. put factual sports reporting on solid First Amendment ground. Team color pairs plus abbreviations are the lowest-risk option: color schemes were protected in Smack Apparel only in combination with other school indicia on merchandise, not colors in the abstract, and Sportradar/SportsDataIO both ship team hex colors (SportsDataIO with a "not licensed for commercial use" caveat).
research.recommendation:
Ordered from lowest to highest risk and cost (describing what the sources support, not legal advice):

1. Default: own marks. Team abbreviation or nickname text on a two-color chip from the team's palette (what TEAM_COLORS/countryColorPair already do). Cost $0. Word marks used to identify a game are the core nominative-fair-use case (New Kids, Volkswagenwerk); Smack Apparel protected colors only in combination with school indicia on fan merchandise, and no case treats UI color chips in a factual scores display as infringement. Keep an "all team names and marks belong to their owners; not affiliated with any league" line in Terms. This is also what App Review responders suggest ("alternative visual identifiers") and it sidesteps 5.2.1 entirely, which matters because Apple does not entertain fair-use arguments, only letterhead authorization.

2. Athlete photos via Wikimedia Commons CC files, extended from tennis to all sports, with two fixes to tennis_photos.js: (a) resolve through the Commons file API and store license + author + file page URL, skip non-free/fair-use files, and render the credit (a small "Photo: Author, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons" caption or an /image-credits page linked from the avatar); (b) show photos only inside factual game/score/record surfaces, never in paywall, push, OG share cards or marketing (3344(d) sports-account exemption, Gionfriddo, C.B.C. cover reporting; Commons warns advertising-type use needs subject consent). Cost $0. Residual risk: personality-rights claims, low in a stats context per the sources.

3. Stop serving a.espncdn.com headshots and never add ESPN logos. Disney's terms limit ESPN content to personal noncommercial use, ban automated extraction and "building a business" on it, and 5.2.2 requires you to be "specifically permitted" under the third-party service's terms with authorization on request. Replace the ESPN branch in tennis_photos.js with Commons-only; delete the espncdn templates in mock_live.js when the mocks are next touched.

4. If real headshots with clean transparent backgrounds become a product need: SportsDataIO Official/Converted Headshots or Getty Editorial ($167/mo for 10 downloads, editorial-only, roughly $17/image at that tier; not scalable to full rosters) via sales quotes. Ask each vendor in writing whether a betting-information publisher (not an operator) is an approved use; Sportradar's Images API is explicitly "prohibited for betting clients" and Stats Perform bars betting use and commercial use of headshots, so expect refusals or custom paper. Budget guess $500-1,000+/mo (third-party estimate, not verified).

5. Real league logos: highest risk, highest cost. Nominative fair use is weakest for stylized logos (Tabari: "visual trappings"), illustrated logos also carry copyright, NCAA has litigated betting-adjacent mark use, every data vendor disclaims logo rights (Sportradar 2.9, SportsDataIO "not licensed for public or commercial use", Sportmonks, API-Football, TheSportsDB), and App Review has documented rejections for NBA, FIFA and club logos with only two exits: rights documents or removal. No league publishes a small-media digital logo license; the visible programs (NFL Properties, NBA Properties, CLC) are merchandise-shaped with minimum guarantees and years-in-business screens (NFL figures around $100k/yr reported secondhand, not verified). Sports-Reference's "we use them under a fair use argument, small resolution, educational" stance is the realistic web-only posture some large sites take, but it does not transfer to the iOS app. If logos are ever pursued, do it web-only, small size, identification-only, and keep the app on own marks.

findings.finding: Ninth Circuit New Kids on the Block test (971 F.2d 302, 1992): a third party may use another's mark if (1) the product is not readily identifiable without the mark, (2) only so much of the mark as is reasonably necessary is used, and (3) nothing suggests sponsorship or endorsement. The Second Circuit (2016) folds the same factors into its Polaroid confusion analysis rather than treating it as a standalone defense, so outcomes vary by circuit.

verdicts.reason:
Not refuted; claim holds against primary sources, with one small precision note.

Primary source 1: the Second Circuit's own opinion, Int'l Info. Sys. Sec. Certification Consortium v. Security University, No. 14-3456 (2d Cir. May 18, 2016), 823 F.3d 153 (govinfo PDF). It quotes the New Kids test verbatim (971 F.2d at 308): (1) product or service "not readily identifiable without use of the trademark"; (2) "only so much of the mark or marks may be used as is reasonably necessary"; (3) user "must do nothing that would, in conjunction with the mark, suggest sponsorship or endorsement." It then holds: "nominative fair use is not an affirmative defense to a claim of infringement under the Lanham Act" and "in cases involving nominative use, in addition to considering the Polaroid factors, courts are to consider (1)...(2)...(3)..." with three factors tracking New Kids. The court also states the district court "erred in applying solely the Ninth Circuit's test... instead of applying our Court's Polaroid test." That matches the claim's characterization.

Primary source 2: Ninth Circuit Model Civil Jury Instruction 15.26 (cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov) states the same three elements, confirming the factor wording.

Cited source (Arnold & Porter, Nov. 2016) supports the claim: Ninth Circuit test replaces likelihood-of-confusion analysis; Third Circuit treats it as a true affirmative defense; Second Circuit integrates the New Kids factors into Polaroid. Mondaq mirror of the same article confirms the three-way split.

Precision notes (do not rise to refutation): (a) the Second Circuit's factors are lightly reworded, not identical: factor 1 asks whether the mark is "necessary to describe both the plaintiff's product or service and the defendant's product or service," and factor 3 adds whether the defendant's conduct "reflects the true or accurate relationship" between the products; (b) in the Ninth Circuit the New Kids test is not technically an affirmative defense either (per instruction 15.26 the plaintiff bears the burden of showing the use is not nominative); it is a substitute confusion test. The claim's "standalone defense" shorthand is loose but commonly used. No newer authority found overruling ISC2 or New Kids as of 2026-09-15 (not exhaustively verified).

Could not refute; the claim checks out against primary sources. (1) New Kids on the Block v. News America Publishing, 971 F.2d 302 (9th Cir., decided 1992-07-24), text via Harvard Caselaw Access Project (https://static.case.law/f2d/971/cases/0302-01.json): the court holds "a commercial user is entitled to a nominative fair use defense provided he meets the following three requirements" and states them exactly as claimed (not readily identifiable without the mark; only so much as is reasonably necessary; nothing suggesting sponsorship or endorsement). (2) Second Circuit, Int'l Info. Sys. Sec. Certification Consortium v. Security University, 823 F.3d 153, decided 2016-05-18, verified from the court's own slip opinion on govinfo (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCOURTS-ca2-14-03456/pdf/USCOURTS-ca2-14-03456-0.pdf) and CAP (https://static.case.law/f3d/823/cases/0153-01.json): "nominative fair use is not an affirmative defense to a claim of infringement under the Lanham Act" and "in nominative use cases, in addition to considering the Polaroid factors, courts are to consider (1)...(2)...(3)" the three New Kids-derived factors; it also says "we see no reason to replace the Polaroid test." That is precisely "folds the factors into Polaroid rather than a standalone defense." (3) The cited Arnold & Porter piece says exactly this and describes the three-way split (9th replaces the confusion test, 3d treats it as an affirmative defense, 2d hybrid). Independent secondary confirmation: Kilpatrick alert noting SCOTUS denied cert in 2017 so "the various approaches ... will remain" (https://ktslaw.com/en/Insights/Alert/2017/1/Circuit-Split-Remains-SCOTUS-Passes-on-Defining-Nominative-Fair-Use). Minor glosses only: the Second Circuit slightly rewords factor 1 ("necessary to describe both the plaintiff's product ... and the defendant's product") and drops "reasonably" from factor 2, so "the same factors" is close but not verbatim; and "outcomes vary by circuit" is a fair inference from the acknowledged split rather than a holding. Neither undermines the claim.

findings.topic: Nominative fair use: logos vs names
findings.finding: Toyota v. Tabari, 610 F.3d 1171 (9th Cir. 2010): the court held that using the stylized Lexus mark and the 'Lexus L' logo went beyond what nominative use allows because 'The Tabaris could adequately communicate their message without using the visual trappings of the Lexus brand.' Plain word marks in text satisfied the test; the logo did not. The same principle traces to Volkswagenwerk v. Church, 411 F.2d 350 (9th Cir. 1969), where an independent repair shop could say 'Volkswagen' but the court noted it did not adopt VW's distinctive lettering or emblem (emblem detail not verified from primary text; the holding on the word mark is verified).

verdicts.reason: Not refuted. Both primary sources support the claim. (1) Toyota v. Tabari, 610 F.3d 1171, cited PDF at cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov (slip op. pp. 9713-15): "Toyota suggests that use of the stylized Lexus mark and 'Lexus L' logo was more use of the mark than necessary and suggested sponsorship or endorsement by Toyota. This is true: The Tabaris could adequately communicate their message without using the visual trappings of the Lexus brand. New Kids, 971 F.2d at 308 n.7. Moreover, those visual cues might lead some consumers to believe they were dealing with an authorized Toyota affiliate." The court then noted the stylized mark and L logo were gone by trial and replaced with a disclaimer, and that use of the plain word Lexus in domain names/text was nominative fair use; disposition VACATED AND REMANDED. Minor caveat: the logo statement is the court agreeing with Toyota's point in the course of the New Kids analysis, and the injunction outcome turned on the changed site, so "held" is slightly strong but not wrong. (2) Volkswagenwerk v. Church, 411 F.2d 350, 352 (9th Cir. 1969), primary text via Caselaw Access Project (https://static.case.law/f2d/411/cases/0350-01.json): "Another was the fact that Church did not use Volkswagen's distinctive lettering style or color scheme, nor did he display the encircled 'VW' emblem." The emblem/lettering detail the claim flagged as unverified is now verified from the opinion text. Note Tabari itself cites Church for the "Independent" disclaimer point and the sandwich-board/necessity point (411 F.2d at 352), not for the emblem detail; the claim does not assert otherwise. Independent secondary confirmation: Justia listing https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F2/411/350/424107/ (403 to fetch, but search snippet matched the same language).

Not refuted; the claim is substantively accurate with one wording caveat. (1) The cited Ninth Circuit PDF (07-55344) and an independent copy on FindLaw both contain the quoted language verbatim: "Toyota suggests that use of the stylized Lexus mark and 'Lexus L' logo was more use of the mark than necessary and suggested sponsorship or endorsement by Toyota. This is true: The Tabaris could adequately communicate their message without using the visual trappings of the Lexus brand" (citing New Kids, 971 F.2d at 308 n.7). The court added that "Imagery, logos and other visual markers may be particularly significant in cyberspace." Caveat: calling this a "holding" is slightly strong. The Tabaris had already removed the stylized mark and L logo by trial and replaced them with a disclaimer; the disposition was vacate and remand with instructions on the scope of the injunction, so the logo passage functions as guidance for the remand rather than the dispositive holding (which was that the injunction was overbroad and nominative use of the plain word "Lexus" in domain names is permissible). The "plain word marks satisfy, logo does not" framing is a fair summary. (2) Volkswagenwerk v. Church: Tabari cites it only for the mechanic's sign ("we affirmed the right of a mechanic to put up a sign advertising that he specialized in repairing Volkswagen cars... 411 F.2d at 352"); the Tabari opinion never mentions lettering or emblem, so the emblem detail does not come from Tabari. However, the Volkswagenwerk opinion itself does contain the sentence "Church did not use Volkswagen's distinctive lettering style or color scheme, nor did he display the encircled 'VW' emblem" (411 F.2d at 352), confirmed via a secondary source (DuetsBlog quoting the opinion) and search snippets of the Justia/OpenJurist copies; Justia, OpenJurist and CourtListener returned 403 so the primary text is not directly verified here, consistent with the claim's own "not verified" flag. Sources: https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2010/07/08/07-55344.pdf ; https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/us-9th-circuit/1530600.html ; https://www.duetsblog.com/2020/03/articles/advertising/nominative-fair-use-of-anothers-logo/ ; https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F2/411/350/424107/ (403, snippet only).

findings.topic: Nominative fair use: practitioner view for scores/news sites
findings.finding: Attorney Q&A on Avvo consistently says team NAMES for schedules/scores are low risk, logos are 'less necessary' than names, some argue reporting-context logo use is nominative fair use, and a key caveat: 'Logos are protected by Copyright and nominative fair use under trademark law will not solve the problem of copyright infringement.' Threads specifically about live-scores apps note clubs often do not answer permission requests.

verdicts.reason:
Partially refuted: the general thrust is supported, but the "key caveat" quote is not in the cited source and is contradicted within the same Avvo Q&A body. Verified by opening four Avvo threads in the browser (WebFetch/curl get 403).

Supported:
- Names low risk / logos "more than necessary": cited thread 2577626 (May 2016): Sack: "Only use team names"; Natoli: logos are "often considered to be more than what is necessary... always more exposure when you use a company's logo... as opposed to just their text name." Thread 878285 (2012, scores/schedules app): Ross: scores/schedules are facts, "limited, 'nominative'" use of team names OK, "Don't use logos or team colors." Thread 4775571 (2020, soccer scores app): Natoli: "fine using the team names... in text"; logos "may be considered more than what is needed."
- Some argue nominative fair use covers logo use in commentary context: Natoli (2577626) and Koslyn (2577626, no-commerce blog).

Not supported / contradicted:
- The quoted caveat "Logos are protected by Copyright and nominative fair use under trademark law will not solve the problem of copyright infringement" does NOT appear in the cited thread 2577626, nor in threads 6024264, 878285, 4775571. A web search for the exact phrase returns no Avvo hit. Worse, in the cited thread Natoli says the opposite ("I think it would cleanly fall under a fair use scenario regards to copyright as well"), and in the live-scores thread 6024264 (Jun 2024) Koslyn (voted Most Helpful) says "Logos are protected by trademark law, not copyright law, although many trademark rightsholders do register their logos for copyrights." So Avvo attorneys are not "consistent" on the copyright point; the claim's caveat is unattributed and mischaracterizes the consensus.
- "Consistently": the cited thread itself has 6 answers split between flat "No, you cannot use logos" (Vaccaro, Riechelson, Sack, Ross) and "little risk"/fair use (Natoli, Koslyn). Ross explicitly says fair use/First Amendment is "highly unlikely" to protect logo use.
- "Clubs often do not answer permission requests": this appears only as the ASKER's statement in thread 6024264 ("the ones I contacted do not even reply"), not an attorney observation. Attorney replies there: news outlets may show logos, "Commercial sites need licenses" (Koslyn); logos often not needed, describe in text (Natoli).

Sources: https://www.avvo.com/legal-answers/can-i-use-the-logos-of-teams-from-nfl-mlb-etc-on-m-2577626.html ; https://www.avvo.com/legal-answers/how-do-live-scores-apps-sites-get-permission-to-us-6024264.html ; https://www.avvo.com/legal-answers/do-i-need-an-nfl-license-or-nba-license-to-show-sc-878285.html ; https://www.avvo.com/legal-answers/can-i-use-team-logos-on-an-app-i-create-if-the-app-4775571.html . Justia/JustAnswer independent threads returned 403 (not verified).

Partly supported, but the claim is overstated and its key quote is not in the cited source. What checks out (Avvo, opened directly): in the cited 2016 blog thread (avvo.com/.../2577626) Natoli says using logos "is often considered to be more than what is necessary" and text names carry less exposure under nominative fair use, and Sack says "Only use team names"; in the 2019 reporting-app thread (avvo.com/legal-answers/can-i-use-sports-team-logo-on-my-app-for-reporting-4736850.html) Natoli says a logo used to illustrate a Giants game report "is likely not an issue"; in the 2024 live-scores thread (avvo.com/legal-answers/how-do-live-scores-apps-sites-get-permission-to-us-6024264.html) the ASKER (not an attorney) says contacted clubs "do not even reply", and in the 2024 soccer-prediction thread (avvo.com/legal-answers/how-can-i-use-soccer-club-logos-on-my-application--5983002.html) the asker says clubs refuse. What fails: (1) The quoted caveat "Logos are protected by Copyright and nominative fair use under trademark law will not solve the problem of copyright infringement" appears in none of the five Avvo threads opened (cited thread + 4 related) and a web search for the exact phrase returns zero hits; not verified. Worse, in the live-scores thread Koslyn states the opposite framing: "Logos are protected by trademark law, not copyright law" (adding owners often also register copyrights for fee-shifting). The nearest real statement is Koslyn's soccer-thread line that unpermitted use invites suit for trademark infringement, dilution, unfair competition "and copyright infringement." (2) "Consistently" is wrong: in the cited thread 4 of 6 attorneys say flatly no logos without permission, Ross says fair use is "highly unlikely" for a blog, Natoli says "little risk" in practice, Koslyn says a non-commercial no-ads site is fine; the 2013 NBA thread (avvo.com/legal-answers/can-i-use-the-nba-logo--team-logos--players-names--1149141.html) is 5 of 5 "not without permission" while allowing scores/stats. Advice is split, not consistent. (3) The cited URL is a 2016 blog thread, not a live-scores-app thread, and it contains nothing about clubs ignoring permission requests. Note: Avvo (Cloudflare-gated) was read via the browser pane; comments on answers were not expanded, so the quote could conceivably sit in a collapsed comment, but no evidence found.

findings.finding: Wikimedia Legal: US logos are copyrightable only above a threshold of originality; 'words and short phrases, titles, slogans, familiar symbols or designs, or mere variations of typographic ornamentation' do not qualify, while illustrated logos (most pro/college mascot logos) easily do. Trademark protection is independent of copyright. Practical read: wordmark/letter logos may be copyright-free but still trademarked; illustrated crests carry both.

verdicts.reason: Not refuted. The cited Wikilegal page (last edited 2024-01-05, explicitly "not legal advice") supports each element: it says there is no special threshold for logos, they need a "minimal quantum of personal creativity"; it lists the exact ineligible elements the claim quotes ("words and short phrases, titles, slogans, familiar symbols or designs, or mere variations of typographic ornamentation, lettering or coloring"); it says illustrations "easily meet the threshold of originality under U.S. copyright law"; and it states copyright and trademark are "entirely separate" regimes. Independent primary sources confirm: 37 CFR 202.1(a) excludes "Words and short phrases such as names, titles, and slogans; familiar symbols or designs; mere variations of typographic ornamentation, lettering or coloring" (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/37/202.1), and the US Copyright Office FAQ states "Copyright does not protect names, titles, slogans, or short phrases" but "copyright protection may be available for logo artwork that contains sufficient authorship" and "an artistic logo may also be protected as a trademark" (copyright.gov/help/faq/faq-protect.html). Two caveats, neither fatal: (1) the "most pro/college mascot logos" phrasing is the claim author's inference; the Wikilegal page speaks of illustrations generally, not sports mascots specifically. (2) The page notes that combinations of unprotectable elements CAN qualify if "numerous enough" and originally arranged (Ninth Circuit, roughly more than six elements) and that the Copyright Office registers more liberally than courts rule, so a stylized wordmark is not automatically copyright-free; the claim's hedge "may be copyright-free" is consistent with this. Circular 33 text could not be extracted from the PDF (not verified), but the FAQ covers the same ground.

Not refuted. The cited Wikimedia Legal page (https://meta.wikimedia.org/wiki/Wikilegal/Copyright_threshold_of_originality_for_logos) supports every element: it applies the Feist "minimal quantum of creativity" threshold to logos, quotes 37 CFR 202.1 for the excluded categories ("words and short phrases, titles, slogans, familiar symbols or designs, or mere variations of typographic ornamentation, lettering or coloring"), states that "Illustrations ... easily meet the threshold of originality under U.S. copyright law," and separates the regimes ("trademark law is used to protect the association between a logo and products or services, while copyright protects the artistic work expressed in the logo"). Independent primary source confirms the exclusion list verbatim: 37 CFR 202.1(a) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/37/202.1) lists "Words and short phrases such as names, titles, and slogans; familiar symbols or designs; mere variations of typographic ornamentation, lettering or coloring." US Copyright Office Circular 33 (https://www.copyright.gov/circs/circ33.pdf) restates the same categories as unprotectable (full quote extraction from the PDF not verified). Two minor caveats, neither rising to refutation: (a) "most pro/college mascot logos easily do" is the claimant's practical inference, not a statement on the Wikimedia page, which speaks of illustrations generally; (b) the page adds a nuance the claim omits: uncopyrightable elements can still combine into a copyrightable whole if "numerous enough and their selection and arrangement original enough," so a complex letter/wordmark design is not automatically copyright-free.

findings.topic: How a large stats site handles logos (Sports-Reference)
findings.finding: Sports-Reference (2016 redesign) uses logos aggregated by SportsLogos.net under an agreement with Chris Creamer, and states: 'Obviously, we do not own these logos and cannot give you permission to use them. We use them under a fair use argument. We use small resolution images... And we provide them for educational purposes only.' This is a self-described fair-use bet by a large, lawyered, ad-supported site, not a league license.

verdicts.reason: Not refuted. The cited source supports the claim verbatim. Fetched via curl (WebFetch got 403): the post "Redesign: Team and League Logos Courtesy SportsLogos.net", posted by sean (Sean Forman) on June 19, 2016, says Sports-Reference "worked out an agreement" with Chris Creamer during the 2016 redesign to use copies of his aggregated logos, and contains the exact quoted passage: "Obviously, we do not own these logos and cannot give you permission to use them. We use them under a fair use argument. We use small resolution images, which do not impact the economic viability of the logos for their owners. And we provide them for educational purposes only." Independent confirmation that the position is still current: a live Baseball-Reference team page (https://www.baseball-reference.com/teams/NYY/2025.shtml, fetched 2026-09-15) carries the footer "Logos were compiled by the amazing SportsLogos.net" and "All logos are the trademark & property of their owners and not Sports Reference LLC. We present them here for purely educational purposes." No league license is mentioned anywhere on either page. Minor nuances the claim omits: the post adds "since I'm not a lawyer, this is clearly not legal advice," and the "lawyered" characterization is an inference (not verified from a primary source); "ad-supported" is consistent with ad slots present in the fetched page markup. SportsLogos.net's own FAQ did not surface any statement on the arrangement (not verified from their side).

Could not refute. The cited source (Sports-Reference blog, "Redesign: Team and League Logos Courtesy SportsLogos.net", posted by sean, June 19, 2016) contains the quoted passages verbatim: an agreement with Chris Creamer/SportsLogos.net to "use copies of his aggregated logos on our site," and "Obviously, we do not own these logos and cannot give you permission to use them. We use them under a fair use argument. We use small resolution images, which do not impact the economic viability of the logos for their owners. And we provide them for educational purposes only." (fetched via curl; WebFetch returned 403). Independent confirmation: the current live site footer on baseball-reference.com team pages and sports-reference.com/about (Copyright 2000-2026) still reads "All logos are the trademark & property of their owners and not Sports Reference LLC. We present them here for purely educational purposes... Logos were compiled by the amazing SportsLogos.net," and team pages carry a "via Sports Logos.net / About logos" credit, so the stance is not outdated. Minor caveat: "not a league license" is the claimant's inference; the post never mentions any league license, and the disclaimer that SR cannot grant permission is consistent with there being none, but the absence of a league license is not affirmatively stated by SR (not verified beyond that). Also note a March 23, 2017 update in the post: SR removed logos displayed for seasons before the earliest available logo, which does not affect the claim.

findings.finding: SportsLogos.net states it 'does not own any of the team, league or event logos/uniforms depicted within this site and does not have the power to grant usage rights to anyone'; the site is 'maintained for research, educational, and historical purposes only.' It is a source of image files, not of rights.

verdicts.reason: Not refuted. The cited source supports the claim nearly verbatim. The homepage footer at https://www.sportslogos.net/ currently reads: "SportsLogos.Net does not own any of the team, league or event logos/uniforms depicted within this site, we do not have the power to grant usage rights to anyone" and "This site is maintained for research, educational, and historical purposes only, do not abuse it." Independent corroboration from the site's own FAQ (https://www.sportslogos.net/faq/): "we're not able to grant anyone permission to use these graphics for commercial purposes," logos "are properties of their respective leagues, teams, ownership groups and/or organizations," and merchandise use requires contacting the league or team directly; the site also withholds vector/high-res files citing counterfeiters. The About page (https://www.sportslogos.net/about) carries the same ownership disclaimer per search snippet. Minor wording note: the claim paraphrases "we do not have the power" as "does not have the power," which is immaterial. The conclusion that the site supplies image files but no rights is consistent with every primary statement found. Third-party independent commentary was not verified, but the provider's own pages are the primary source for what the site states.

Not refuted. The cited source (https://www.sportslogos.net/) carries the quoted disclaimer verbatim in its footer: "SportsLogos.Net does not own any of the team, league or event logos/uniforms depicted within this site, we do not have the power to grant usage rights to anyone... this site is maintained for research, educational, and historical purposes only, do not abuse it." The same text appears across the site's league/sport index pages (e.g. https://www.sportslogos.net/teams/list_by_league/4/Major-League-Baseball-Logos/MLB-Logos/). The site's own FAQ (https://www.sportslogos.net/faq/) independently confirms and strengthens the claim: no affiliation with leagues/teams, cannot grant permission for commercial use, merchandise users must contact the league or team, and no vector/high-res files are supplied. Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SportsLogos.net) confirms it is a privately run Canadian archive "devoted to the display and study of sports logos" founded by Chris Creamer, with no mention of any licensing role. Minor precision note: the claim's paraphrase "does not have the power" matches the site's "we do not have the power"; the characterization "a source of image files, not of rights" is the claimant's inference, but it is consistent with the FAQ. No third-party primary source (statute or court opinion) was found on this point; not verified beyond the site's own statements and Wikipedia.

findings.topic: How Wikipedia handles logos (the most conservative free-content model)
findings.finding: Wikipedia treats illustrated team logos as non-free content usable only in the infobox of the article about that team under a per-use fair-use rationale; 'Outside of these limits, neither non-free nor trademarked logos should be used within an article,' i.e. never as icons in lists, tables or schedules. Logos below the copyright threshold (text/simple shapes) are treated as free for copyright but 'a logo can still be protected by trademark law.' An RFC noted NFL logos being used 100+ times across season pages as a policy problem. Bottom line: the icon-in-a-scores-table use is exactly what Wikipedia's rules disallow.

findings.topic: Do leagues license logos to small apps? NFL
findings.finding: NFL Properties runs a pre-qualification program aimed at product licensees; secondary sources report screens of ~3 years manufacturing/distribution experience, two years of audited financials, a minimum annual royalty guarantee around $100,000 paid on signing, and $6M/$12M liability insurance. The NFL pre-qual page itself returned 404 when checked and UpCounsel now warns not to rely on fixed figures, so the numbers are not verified against a current primary source. No public NFL program for small digital/media logo licenses was found.

findings.topic: Do leagues license logos to small apps? NBA / MLB / NHL
findings.finding: NBA Properties licenses names/logos/uniforms with royalties on net sales plus an annual minimum guarantee and a questionnaire on years in operation and distribution (merchandise-oriented; archived license agreements show the structure). MLB Properties (formed 1966) and MLB Players Inc. (player group rights) use advance and guaranteed minimum compensation. NHL's copyright page: team logos 'may not be reproduced without the prior written consent of NHL Enterprises, L.P.' with only a DMCA agent contact, no permission form. No league publishes a small-media digital logo license; all routes are contact-sales with minimum guarantees.

findings.topic: Do leagues license logos to small apps? College (CLC)
findings.finding: CLC (200+ schools, NCAA, conferences) offers Retail and Internal license categories built around products; application fee $250 first school + $125 each additional, royalties typically 8-12% of wholesale, artwork delivered via Logos on Demand only after licensing. No digital-media-only category is described; 'contact CLC' for other uses.

NCAA sued DraftKings over 'March Madness', 'Final Four' etc. in its betting app, stating that 'sports betting must not be associated with, endorsed by, or linked to NCAA championships,' and sends cease-and-desist letters each tournament season. Relevance: a betting-information product using NCAA/school marks has a more hostile rights-holder than a general scores app.

ESPN sites and apps are governed by Disney's Terms of Use, which grant only a 'limited, non-exclusive, non-sublicensable, non-transferable license... for your personal, noncommercial use only,' with 'no right to reproduce, distribute, communicate to the public,' a ban on accessing or extracting content 'using a robot, spider, script, or other automated means,' and a ban on any 'commercial or business-related use' or building 'a business utilizing the Disney Products.' Hot-linking a.espncdn.com headshots/logos from a paid product is not covered by any grant. ESPN retired its public API in Dec 2014; site.api.espn.com endpoints are undocumented internal endpoints.

findings.topic: ESPN CDN: what the site does today
findings.finding: Local code already depends on a.espncdn.com: src/tennis_photos.js HEAD-checks and stores https://a.espncdn.com/i/headshots/tennis/players/full/{id}.png as home_photo/away_photo, and src/mock_live.js templates NFL/MLB headshot URLs. Those URLs are served to end users, so the Disney terms above apply to that usage.

5.2.1: 'Don't use protected third-party material such as trademarks, copyrighted works, or patented ideas in your app without permission... Apps should be submitted by the person or legal entity that owns or has licensed the intellectual property.' 5.2.2: if your app displays content from a third-party service, 'ensure that you are specifically permitted to do so under the service's terms of use. Authorization must be provided upon request.' 4.1(c) (Nov 2025) added an explicit ban on using another's brand in icon or name.

findings.topic: App Store: documented rejections for league/team logos
findings.finding: Apple Developer Forums thread 699048: a football app on a bug-fix resubmission was rejected (Guideline 4.1) for content that 'resembles one or multiple third-party sports teams and/or leagues'; Apple's two options were documentary evidence of rights in App Review Information (with a warning that falsified docs mean account termination) or removal of all team/league content. The developer noted v1 had been approved 8 months earlier; a responder suggested alternative visual identifiers for teams.

findings.topic: App Store: documented rejections (FIFA / club logos, betting app)
findings.finding: Thread 718427: a free World Cup 2022 / European league score-betting app was rejected under 5.2.1 for the FIFA logo and club logos sourced from api-football; the developer removed the FIFA logo and disabled club logos and names pending a fix. An Apple staffer told him to read the API provider's terms about permitted use of logos and images, i.e. the API vendor's 'we only provide the sources' disclaimer did not help.

findings.topic: App Store: NBA logos and player images
findings.finding: Thread 130430 (NBA trade-machine app): responders stated developers are 'obligated to show proof-of-right' for content they do not own, 'a simple disclaimer is no substitute,' and other apps' approval is not precedent. One responder argued team logos and player images need explicit permission and suggested an attorney letter to App Review. Third-party guidance: App Review accepts 'a PDF on the rights holder's letterhead'; fair-use arguments do not work with reviewers.

Offers headshots (incl. transparent premium), coach/venue images, action shots (Getty/USA Today/Reuters/AP), team and league logos, and flags; 'over 100 image collections... from four different providers.' Hard restrictions: 'Sportradar's Images API is for media use only. Use of this API is prohibited for betting clients.' Sportradar T&C 2.10: no use 'in connection with... any gambling or betting-related purposes without express written approval'; 2.9: 'Nothing herein shall be deemed to confer to Customer any license... to use logos... belonging to the sports league.' No public pricing; contact mediasupport@sportradar.com. Third-party estimate for this tier is $500-$1,000+/month (not verified).

Sells Official Headshots (NFL/NBA/MLB/NHL studio shots via licensed third parties, transparent) and Converted Headshots (IMAGN action crops, big four + golf); no public price, sales@sportsdata.io. Its Teams endpoint fields WikipediaLogoUrl and WikipediaWordMarkUrl are described as 'The link to the team's logo hosted on Wikipedia (This is not licensed for public or commercial use)', and even PrimaryColor/SecondaryColor hex fields carry the same '(This is not licensed for public or commercial use)' caveat. So the logos are pointers to Wikipedia files with no rights attached.

Master Licence Agreement 4(k): 'If the Licensed Materials contain any photos/headshots, Licensee shall not use such photos/headshots for any commercial purposes' and they may only be shown alongside the delivered materials; 4(m): no use for Betting Activities or supply to Betting Entities; 4(e)(i): licensee 'may need to obtain a Direct Use License' from rights holders at its own cost. Pricing is custom quote; they say they work with startups.

findings.topic: Other sports APIs: logos come with no rights
findings.finding: Sportmonks FAQ: 'All logo's and profile photos are copyrighted by their legal owner'; customers must 'arrange the proof of intellectual property yourself.' API-Football: logos/images provided 'solely for identification and descriptive purposes,' rights held by leagues/clubs (secondary summary, page fetch blocked). TheSportsDB ($9/mo dev, $20/mo small business): artwork is mostly user-made fan art, 'trademarked sports logos must be used As is', free tier bars app-store publication, DMCA takedowns honored within 24h; it grants no league rights.

Getty plans page: Editorial subscription $167/month for 10 downloads, 'Editorial use only' (news, sports, entertainment + archive); Creative $225/month for 10 (commercial). UltraPack 5-pack $1,400 ($280/image); 'Editorial photos cannot be used for commercial purposes with UltraPacks.' Legal coverage up to $10,000 per file. Practical read: roughly $17/headshot at the low tier, editorial context only, and per-image licensing does not scale to thousands of active players; enterprise/API is custom quote.

AP offers PhotoChoice Access (metered monthly subscription by image tier), Photo Microfeeds (API/XML by topic incl. sports), RF and RM creative licenses; rights are non-transferable and cannot be sublicensed. No public prices; sales quote.

findings.topic: Wikimedia Commons athlete photos: copyright side
findings.finding: CC BY and CC BY-SA both allow commercial reuse. Required: credit the author/licensor, link the license, indicate if changes were made; ShareAlike only bites on derivative works ('if you modify the work, your modifications must also be similarly freely licensed'). Commons does not settle whether a crop counts as a derivative (it points to Commons:Derivative works); resizing a thumbnail is generally treated as not creating a new work but that is not verified from a Commons policy line. Commons provides a ready-made attribution pop-up per file. Note: the Wikipedia REST summary thumbnail the site fetches can be a non-free fair-use image on some articles (rare for living athletes, since Wikipedia does not accept non-free images of living people), so checking the file's license via the Commons API before display is the safe pattern.

findings.topic: Wikimedia Commons athlete photos: personality rights side
findings.finding: Commons: 'non-copyright restrictions may apply... commercial use of images of people may require the explicit agreement of the subject, and not just the agreement of the image creator.' In the US 'consent is not as a rule required to photograph people in public places,' but 'Commercial use (which has a different meaning here than it does for copyright) usually requires consent,' with advertising as the clear example. Commons' own essay says right of publicity 'probably' cannot apply to noncommercial informational content protected by the First Amendment; turning content into an endorsement 'is probably violating the law.'

California Civil Code 3344(d) exempts uses 'in connection with any news, public affairs, or sports broadcast or account.' Gionfriddo v. MLB (Cal. App. 2001) held players' names, statistics, photos and video on MLB websites and programs were protected sports accounts / matters of public interest. C.B.C. Distribution v. MLBAM (8th Cir. 2007) held First Amendment rights trumped players' publicity rights for use of names and stats in a paid fantasy product because the information is public. Caveat from DMLP: the line is drawn at commercial sponsorship/advertising, and a newsworthy subject 'is not automatically privileged' when used commercially; so headshots inside factual score/record displays sit far better than headshots in ads or paywall marketing.

findings.topic: What the site already does for tennis
findings.finding: src/tennis_photos.js resolves ESPN headshot first, then the Wikipedia REST summary thumbnail (with a tennis-description guard), caches to tennis_player_photos, and stamps today_games.home_photo/away_photo (~77% coverage). It stores only the image URL; it does not capture the Commons file license or author, so attribution required by CC BY/BY-SA is not currently rendered, and it does not distinguish CC files from non-free ones. The frontend falls back to flag/initials (utils.tennisAvatar).

Board of Supervisors (LSU et al.) v. Smack Apparel, 550 F.3d 465 (5th Cir. 2008): unregistered school color schemes were protectable, but the court stressed 'the claimed trademark is in the colors on merchandise that combines other identifying indicia referring to the Universities' and considered 'not only the color but also the entire context' of fan apparel; colors in the abstract were not what was protected. Boise State separately holds a registered mark for blue artificial turf. Qualitex (1995) allows single-color marks only with secondary meaning and non-functionality. No case was found treating team-color UI chips in a scores/stats display as infringement; the risk vector in the cases is merchandise that trades on fan affinity.

Sportradar and SportsDataIO both distribute team hex colors as data fields; SportsDataIO annotates each color field '(This is not licensed for public or commercial use)', the same caveat it puts on the Wikipedia logo URLs, i.e. the vendor is not warranting rights in colors either. Team colors are also freely listed on Wikipedia team pages and in open-source color packs; the site's existing TEAM_COLORS map in modal.js is the same approach.

Apple's Sports app legal page credits only 'Other company and product names and logos mentioned herein may be trademarks of their respective companies' and identifies no league license, so it cannot be cited as evidence of how leagues license logos to apps; Apple's own scale and deals are not a model for a small LLC.

research.summary: Verified against Apple primary sources as of 2026-09-15: whole-dollar price points exist ($1.00 and $5.00 confirmed by the "every $0.10 up to $10" rule plus Apple's explicit "X.00 endings" statement; $75.00 is very likely available but the $50-$200 increment rule was only found in secondary sources). A 3-day free trial is a standard introductory-offer duration and Apple enforces one intro offer per subscription group per Apple ID. Small Business Program: 15%, under $1M prior-year proceeds across Associated Developer Accounts, Account Holder enrolls, rate starts 15 days after the fiscal month of approval. Consumable day pass is the type Apple forum guidance points to for sub-7-day timed access; App Store Server API + V2 notifications are JWS-signed and need only an In-App Purchase key (.p8), key ID, issuer ID, bundle ID (plus app Apple ID for production verification), no shared secret. In the US, IAP is still required to unlock in-app, but since May 1 2025 US-storefront apps may include links/buttons to web checkout with no entitlement, and no commission has been charged on link-outs to date; Apple's Aug 13 2026 proposal (15%, 5% Small Business) is pending before Judge Gonzalez Rogers and SCOTUS granted cert June 30 2026 (stay denied), so link-out economics are unsettled. Guideline 5.3.4 applies only to real-money wagering apps; an information-only picks app is outside it, but Apple bars gambling-related apps from individual (non-organization) accounts, real gambling content rates 18+, and 5.3 warns of extra review time.
research.recommendation: Product setup: (a) One subscription group, e.g. 'CappingAlpha Access'. Products: com.cappingalpha.access.weekly (1 week, $5.00 US base price, rank 2) and com.cappingalpha.access.annual (1 year, $75.00 if the point is listed under 'See Additional Prices', else $74.99, rank 1 so weekly->annual is an immediate upgrade and annual->weekly a downgrade at renewal). (b) Put the 3-day free trial introductory offer on the weekly product only, all territories; leave annual without an intro offer so the single-intro-per-group rule cannot burn the annual sale, and mirror the web 'first-time only' rule by reading isEligibleForIntroOffer instead of your stripe_customer_id (Apple and Stripe trials cannot be cross-linked). (c) Day pass: consumable com.cappingalpha.daypass at $1.00; on purchase send the JWS to the server, verify with SignedDataVerifier / Get Transaction Info, stamp subscription_expires = purchaseDate + 24h on the CappingAlpha user, then finish the transaction; store transaction ids for idempotency and refunds; paywall copy: 'Unlocks every pick for 24 hours from purchase. Does not renew.' (d) Enroll the LLC in the Small Business Program from the Account Holder login before the first App Store sale (rate applies 15 days after the fiscal month of approval); list any other Apple accounts you control. (e) Server: add an In-App Purchase key (.p8, key ID, issuer ID) and the app Apple ID to env, install @apple/app-store-server-library, expose /api/apple/notify (production + sandbox URLs) and handle SUBSCRIBED, DID_RENEW, DID_CHANGE_RENEWAL_STATUS, DID_FAIL_TO_RENEW, EXPIRED, REFUND; drive tier from Get All Subscription Statuses rather than the client. (f) Keep IAP as the only in-app purchase path for the App Store build; a 'cheaper on the web' link to Stripe is legal on the US storefront today at 0%, but Apple's pending 15%/5% proposal and the SCOTUS case make it a nice-to-have, not a pricing strategy. (g) Submit from the Organization (LLC) account, answer the age questionnaire honestly and expect an 18+ rating, keep the existing 18+ gate, and add an in-app 'information only, no wagers' disclaimer.

findings.finding: Apple's 900-point system increments 'every $0.10 up to $10; every $0.50 between $10 and $50; etc.' and explicitly lets developers 'price products beyond $0.99 or €X.99 endings to incorporate rounded price endings (e.g., X.00 or X.90)'. So $1.00 and $5.00 are valid US price points. App Store Connect shows 25 'most common' points by default (.99 style); click 'See Additional Prices' to reach the .00 points. Up to 800 points by default, 100 more (to $10,000) on request.
findings.confidence: high (Apple newsroom + App Store Connect help: https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-in-app-purchases/set-a-price-for-an-in-app-purchase/)

Claim holds. findings.finding: Apple's own text only says 'etc.' above $50. Secondary sources describe $1 steps from $50 to ~$200, which would include $75.00, and the rounded-ending rule applies to annual plans specifically ('particularly useful for managing bundles and annual plans'). $75.00 as a selectable US point is NOT verified from a primary source; confirm in App Store Connect under 'See Additional Prices' when creating the annual subscription. Fallback is $74.99.
findings.confidence: medium (not verified: $50-$200 increment rule only in secondary coverage, e.g. https://appleinsider.com/articles/22/12/06/apple-adding-hundreds-of-app-store-price-points-as-low-as-029)

verdicts.reason: Not refuted. Checked the cited source and three independent ones. (1) Cited source https://developer.apple.com/news/?id=dbrszv62 (Mar 9, 2023) says exactly "every $0.10 up to $10, every $0.50 between $10 and $50, etc." and nothing about increments above $50, annual plans, or rounded endings. So the claim that Apple's text stops at "etc." is accurate for that page. (2) The "particularly useful for managing bundles and annual plans" quote is Apple's own text, but it lives on the Dec 6, 2022 announcement, not the cited page: https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2022/12/apple-announces-biggest-upgrade-to-app-store-pricing-adding-700-new-price-points/ and https://developer.apple.com/news/?id=qzex35ch ("rounded price endings (e.g., x.00 or x.90), which are particularly useful for managing bundles and annual plans"). Minor overstatement in the claim: Apple frames rounded endings as "particularly useful for" annual plans, not a rule that "applies to annual plans specifically"; the quoted words themselves are accurate. (3) App Store Connect Help https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-pricing/set-a-price confirms the "See Additional Prices" UI (25 shown initially, up to 800 by default, +100 on request to $10,000) but does not publish the list. Core claim stands; one attribution error. (1) Cited source (developer.apple.com/news/?id=dbrszv62) verified: it says price points increase "every $0.10 up to $10, every $0.50 between $10 and $50, etc." and gives NO detail above $50 and NO mention of rounded endings, bundles, or annual plans. That is a use-case note about X.00/X.90 endings generally, not a rule that "applies to annual plans specifically", so that wording is slightly overstated, but it is primary-sourced. (3) Apple's ASC help (developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-pricing/set-a-price/) confirms 800 default price points (+100 on request), the initial 25-point list, and the "See Additional Prices" control, supporting the "confirm in ASC" instruction. (4) $1 steps from $50 to ~$200 appear only in secondary sources (e.g. mirava.io/blog/apple-app-store-price-tiers-how-they-work-2026); no public primary list of the 900 USD points was found (the only public CSV, github.com/danielblazquez/Pricing-matrix-AppStoreConnect, is the 2020 pre-expansion matrix). So "$75.00 as a selectable US point is not verified from a primary source" is correct; it could not be confirmed or refuted here either. Fallback $74.99 is also unverified but consistent with the same secondary sources. findings.finding: Introductory offers on auto-renewable subscriptions come in three types (free trial, pay up front, pay as you go). Free trial durations offered: 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks, 1, 2, 3, 6 months, 1 year. Configure per subscription: App Store Connect > Apps > [app] > Subscriptions > group > subscription > Subscription Prices > View all Subscription pricing > Set up Introductory Offer > pick territories, dates, type Free, duration 3 Days. One current + one future offer per storefront per subscription; offers cannot be edited after creation (delete and recreate). Sandbox changes can take up to 1 hour to appear.

verdicts.reason: Cited source supports the claim on every point. Apple's App Store Connect Help page (fetched 2026-09-15) lists the three types (Free trial / Pay up front / Pay as you go); free trial durations "3 Days, 1 or 2 Weeks, 1, 2, 3, or 6 Months, 1 Year"; the exact path Apps > [app] > Subscriptions > group > subscription > Subscription Prices > View all Subscription pricing > Set up Introductory Offer > territories > dates > type/duration/price > Confirm; "one current and one future introductory offer per storefront"; "introductory offers cannot be edited after creation... delete it and create a new one"; and "It may take up to 1 hour for changes you make to product metadata to appear in the sandbox environment." Independent confirmation: Apple's marketing page https://developer.apple.com/app-store/subscriptions/ describes the same three types and "one introductory offer per subscription group" eligibility; Apple dev forum thread https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/781668 references a 3-day trial on a weekly subscription. One minor caveat, not a refutation: Apple's UI restricts which trial durations are selectable relative to the subscription's standard duration (e.g. 3 days is offered for a 1-week subscription), so the full duration list is not uniformly available on every subscription; the claim does not say otherwise. Cocoacasts (third-party, older) shows a "+ / Create Introductory Offer" button label instead of "Set up Introductory Offer", which reflects an older ASC UI, not an error in the claim. Not verified independently: the "one current + one future per storefront" rule and the no-edit rule appear only in Apple's own help page.

Not refuted. The cited App Store Connect help page (fetched 2026-09-15) supports every element of the claim verbatim: three offer types (free trial, pay up front, pay as you go); free-trial durations 3 days, 1 or 2 weeks, 1/2/3/6 months, 1 year; navigation Apps > [app] > Subscriptions > group > subscription > Subscription Prices > View all Subscription pricing > Set up Introductory Offer, then territories, dates, type, duration; "one current and one future introductory offer per storefront"; "Once you create an introductory offer, you won't be able to edit it... delete it and create a new one"; "It may take up to 1 hour for changes you make to product metadata to appear in the sandbox environment." Independent Apple page (https://developer.apple.com/app-store/subscriptions/) confirms the same three types and that you can create an introductory offer for each subscription per territory, with customers redeemable once per subscription group. Minor nuances not contradicting the claim: the help page also states "one introductory offer for each subscription product" (per storefront framing reconciles this), and the sandbox note applies to product metadata changes generally, not only offers. Could not open the StoreKit "Implementing introductory offers" doc (JS-rendered) - not verified, but not needed.

findings.topic: (2) One introductory offer per subscription group per customer
findings.finding: Apple enforces it: 'Customers can redeem only one introductory offer per subscription group.' New subscribers eligible; lapsed subscribers eligible only if they never used an intro offer on any product in the group; existing subscribers not eligible. Enforcement is per Apple ID by the App Store (check Product.subscription.isEligibleForIntroOffer in StoreKit 2 before showing trial copy). Implication: if both weekly and annual sit in one group with trials, a user who trialed weekly cannot trial annual. This is separate from your Stripe stripe_customer_id guard; Apple cannot see web trials and vice versa.

verdicts.reason: Not refuted. The cited page (https://developer.apple.com/app-store/subscriptions/) says verbatim: "Customers can redeem one introductory offer per subscription group." Apple's StoreKit guide "Implementing introductory offers in your app" (https://developer.apple.com/documentation/storekit/implementing-introductory-offers-in-your-app) states the three eligibility rules almost word for word as claimed: "New subscribers are always eligible." / "Lapsed subscribers who renew are eligible if they haven't previously used an introductory offer for the given product (or any product within the same subscription group)." / "Existing subscribers are not eligible for an introductory offer for any product within the same subscription group ... regardless of whether they consumed an introductory offer in the past." The isEligibleForIntroOffer doc (https://developer.apple.com/documentation/storekit/product/subscriptioninfo/iseligibleforintrooffer) confirms the flag is true "if the customer is eligible for an introductory offer on this auto-renewable subscription, or any auto-renewable subscription in the same subscription group." App Store Connect Help (https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-subscriptions/set-up-introductory-offers-for-auto-renewable-subscriptions) gives the exact weekly-then-annual scenario: "if a customer uses a free trial and then upgrades to a subscription product in the same group that also has a free trial, they aren't eligible for the second offer." Minor nuances, not contradictions: Apple's docs do not literally use the phrase "per Apple ID" (they frame it as per customer/receipt), and Apple advises the app to check eligibility before displaying trial copy rather than relying solely on the store to suppress it. The web-vs-App-Store separation (Apple cannot see Stripe trials) is a logical inference, not verified against a specific Apple statement.

Lapsed subscribers who renew are eligible if they haven't previously used an introductory offer for the given product (or any product within the same subscription group). findings.topic: (3) Small Business Program: eligibility and rate

findings.topic: (5) App Store Server API + V2 notifications, Node setup
findings.finding: verifyReceipt is deprecated; the App Store Server API (Get Transaction Info, Get Transaction History, Get All Subscription Statuses) returns JWS-signed payloads (JWSTransactionDecodedPayload). Requests are authenticated with an ES256 JWT built from an In-App Purchase private key (.p8), claims iss = issuer ID, kid = key ID, aud = 'appstoreconnect-v1', bid = bundle ID, exp <= 1 hour. No shared secret. App Store Server Notifications V2 deliver a signedPayload JWS verified via the x5c chain to Apple's Root CA; configure separate Production and Sandbox URLs in App Store Connect. Apple's official Node library (npm @apple/app-store-server-library) needs: encodedKey (.p8 contents), keyId, issuerId, bundleId, environment for AppStoreServerAPIClient; SignedDataVerifier needs Apple root certificates (Buffer[] from apple.com/certificateauthority), bundleId, appAppleId (required in Production), environment, enableOnlineChecks. Keys are created at Users and Access > Integrations > In-App Purchase (Admin role); the issuer ID appears there. Notification types to handle: SUBSCRIBED, DID_RENEW, DID_CHANGE_RENEWAL_STATUS, DID_FAIL_TO_RENEW, EXPIRED, REFUND, ONE_TIME_CHARGE (consumables). Whether ONE_TIME_CHARGE now fires in production (it launched sandbox-only) is not verified; for the day pass, verify the transaction server-side on purchase via Get Transaction Info rather than relying on the notification.

findings.topic: (6) IAP requirement + US link-out status after Epic v. Apple
findings.finding: IAP is still required to unlock content inside the app (3.1.1 unchanged on that point). But per the April 30, 2025 contempt order, Apple updated 3.1.1, 3.1.1(a), 3.1.3, 3.1.3(a) on May 1, 2025 so that on the United States storefront apps may include buttons, external links and other calls to action to the developer's own web checkout with no entitlement and may say it is cheaper there; current guideline text: 'These entitlements are not required for developers to include buttons, external links, or other calls to action in their United States storefront apps.' Commission status: Apple has collected no commission on US link-out purchases since April 2025. On Dec 11, 2025 the Ninth Circuit affirmed the contempt finding and the no-restrictions-on-links rules but vacated the blanket zero-commission ban as punitive, allowing on remand only a fee covering costs 'genuinely and reasonably necessary' for coordinating external links plus modest IP compensation. On Aug 13, 2026 Apple proposed 15% standard / 10% partner programs and subscription renewals / 5% Small Business Program on link-out sales; Judge Gonzalez Rogers has not ruled. Supreme Court granted Apple's petition June 30, 2026 (question limited to how injunction violations are judged), stay requests denied, argument in the term starting October 2026. Net: link-out is permitted in the US today at 0% commission, but a 5-15% fee is likely within months and the whole regime is under SCOTUS review.

findings.topic: (7) Guideline 5.3 for a no-wagering betting-information app
findings.finding: 5.3.4's licensing / geo-restriction / must-be-free requirements apply to apps that 'offer real money gaming (e.g. sports betting...)'; an app that only sells picks and analysis takes no wagers and is outside 5.3.4 and 5.3.3 (no IAP for gaming credit). 5.3's preamble warns gambling-adjacent apps to 'be prepared for extra time during the review process.' research.summary: Mapped ESPN's free, unauthenticated JSON endpoints for player profile pages across NFL, MLB, NBA, WNBA, NHL, NCAAF, PGA golf and ATP/WTA tennis by fetching one athlete per sport with curl on 2026-09-15. Team sports are fully covered by four hosts: site.web.api.espn.com/apis/common/v3/sports/{sport}/{league}/athletes/{id} (header bio, team, headshot, statsSummary WITH league rank, injuries) plus /overview (season stat line, recent games with per-game stats, next game, per-player news, awards, fantasy/rotowire), /stats (career by season), /splits, /gamelog, /bio (awards + team history); sports.core.api.espn.com for raw bio/refs and per-season stats with rank; site.api.espn.com/apis/site/v2/sports/{sport}/{league}/teams/{teamId}/roster for rosters; site.web.api.espn.com/apis/search/v2?query= for id lookup (numeric id is in the uid a:NNNN and in the headshot image URL). Golf and tennis athletes have no team and no /stats, /splits or usable /gamelog: golf's /overview returns recentTournaments (position, score, round scores), seasonRankings (ranked season stats) and a previous/next tournament; scorecards come from core competitor refs (hole-by-hole). Tennis has only a thin bio (no headshot/flag on the league-scoped core doc; use the unscoped sports/tennis/athletes/{id} doc or the search result), W-L/titles/prize via core season statistics, match results via core season eventlog -> competition (notes carry the score line, linescores per set), and the ATP/WTA rankings feed. Gotchas: site.api.espn.com returns 403 to ANY Mozilla-prefixed UA and to an empty UA even from a residential Mac IP (curl default UA works); site.web.api.espn.com and sports.core.api.espn.com accept every UA tested. The news?athlete= filter is silently ignored (identical output with and without); per-player news must come from /overview.news. Headshots are ESPN-hosted at a.espncdn.com/i/headshots/{league}/players/full/{id}.png (resizable via the /combiner/i?img= proxy); licensing is unknown and not verified.
research.recommendation: Build the profile page on site.web.api.espn.com (UA-agnostic) and sports.core.api.espn.com: (1) resolve ids with /apis/search/v2 (parse uid 'a:NNNN', filter defaultLeagueSlug); (2) header from /apis/common/v3/sports/{sport}/{league}/athletes/{id} (bio, team, jersey, headshot, injuries, statsSummary with rankDisplayValue); (3) Overview tab from /overview (season line, recent games + previous-game stat block, nextGame.league.events[0], per-player news, awards, fantasy); (4) Stats/Splits/Game Log/Bio tabs from /stats, /splits, /gamelog (?season=), /bio; (5) rosters from /apis/site/v2/sports/{sport}/{league}/teams/{teamId}/roster (mirror on site.web.api to dodge the Mozilla-UA 403); (6) previous game box via summary?event={gamelog eventId}. Never rely on news?athlete= (ignored); filter league news on categories[].athleteId or use overview.news. Golf: header + ranked stats from the v3 athlete + /overview (recentTournaments, seasonRankings, nextTournament), scorecards from core competitor score/status/linescores refs; there are no Stats/Splits/Game Log endpoints. Tennis: bio from the unscoped core athlete doc (has headshot/flag), rank from the rankings feed, W-L/titles/prize from core season statistics, results from core season eventlog -> competition notes + linescores; no Stats/Splits/Game Log endpoints. Cache aggressively server-side (one fetch per athlete per few minutes), send a non-Mozilla UA to site.api.espn.com, and treat all headshots as ESPN-owned imagery pending a licensing decision.

designs.rationale: Ledger keeps one flat list of all nine cappers, sorted by NFL money descending, with a radio-driven side filter (All / DAL / CHI / Over / Under) and a six-slot count grid so every slot reads as a slot even when the list is filtered. Each row is a full-width anchor with a chevron, which is the tap affordance and needs no JS. Both sides carry identical row treatment, and counts are plain numbers with no meter. This revision resolves the five layout risks without touching the visual idea: (1) the Covers price string now breaks at a deliberate point ("no price," / "graded at -110") with nowrap on each line, so it is two tidy right-aligned lines under the chip instead of an uncontrolled wrap, and the break collapses back to one line at 560px+ where the column is wider; (2) the filter tabs drop to 12px with 2px side padding, 3px gaps and overflow hidden, which leaves roughly 20px of slack per tab at 362px and clips inside the tab under larger OS text instead of pushing the strip; (3) the middle column gains about 18px (disc 34 to 32, row gap 10 to 8, right padding 10 to 8, chip padding 9 to 8, metric gap 8 to 7) so "22-11 +$188 +14.2% ROI" sits on one line with room to spare; (4) the empty state is now wired with :has(), so a filter whose side has no rows hides the list and shows "No cappers on this side" (harmless no-op on the current fixture, and browsers without :has simply ignore those two rules); (5) role=tablist is replaced with role=group plus the same aria-label, which is the honest semantic for a set of labels driving hidden radios.
designs.free_tier_notes: Free tier renders the identical layout with the same nine rows, the same filter strip, the same six-slot counts and the same money/record/ROI cells. Only the .v1-name cell is redacted per row (a muted placeholder bar the same height as the name, initials disc still shown so the row keeps its shape), and the anchor href points at the subscribe flow instead of the profile. One subscribe prompt sits directly under the list as a single line ("See who is on this game") styled like .v1-empty, never a blur wall or overlay. Counts, slot grid, humility line, unqualified line and Grading Note are always visible to everyone.
designs.graded_state_notes: After the game is final the fragment freezes exactly as it was at kickoff (the count line already says "freezes at kickoff"). Each row's .v1-pchip gains a result state: a green ring plus a small W after the pick text for wins, a red ring plus L for losses, a muted ring plus P for pushes, while the price line stays as recorded so the reader can see the price the grade was struck at. The six-slot grid keeps its counts and appends the result letter next to each slot count. Money, record and ROI cells stay pre-game (they are the capper's NFL ledger going into the game, not updated in place). No sorting change, no side is promoted, the humility line and Grading Note stay verbatim.

layout_risks: Right column .v1-pick is capped at 96px on phones; the price string 'no price, graded at -110' (10.5px) has no nowrap so it wraps to 2-3 right-aligned lines under the pick chip on the three Covers rows. Cosmetic, no overflow.

Filter strip: five nowrap tabs share ~340px (about 66px each); 'Under 1' at 12.5px/600 with 4px side padding fits with only a few px to spare, so larger OS text sizes could clip inside the tab (min-width:0 keeps it from pushing the page wider).

Middle column is ~171px at 362px (22 padding + 34 disc + 30 gaps + 9 chevron + 96 pick). The metrics row '22-11 +$188 +14.2% ROI' is close to that width and may wrap ROI onto its own line; ident row wraps 'Action Network' badge under long names like KnightDasCapital. Both wrap cleanly.
.v1-empty ('No cappers on this side') is permanently display:none and no rule ever shows it; with this fixture no filter is empty so nothing is lost, but the element is dead weight.
role=tablist on a div of labels without role=tab children is an a11y nit only; the hidden radios remain keyboard focusable and the strip gets a focus ring.
critique.design_notes: Clean ledger read: initials disc, name plus source badge, record/money/ROI line, recorded time, pick chip pinned right with chevron, and a compact six-slot count grid above a radio-driven side filter (no JS). Tints are all derived from --accent and --green; the L5 chip is accent-tinted rather than red, which keeps the streak chips from reading as a recommendation. All checks pass: scoped selectors, no style/script, no foreign colors, no forbidden words or em dashes, all nine cappers in money order with the right chips, five required strings verbatim, 14.3 KB total.

designs.rationale:
Same idea as before: the card is a scoreboard. Away on the left, home on the right, over and under below, and each capper sits in the column of the side they took, so the six slots are read as two halves of one line rather than a list. Counts are plain chips, both halves mirror each other, and the cappers inside a column sort by NFL money then win percentage.

Revision notes. The kickoff time, venue, and team records all come straight from the fixture (game.start, game.venue, game.awayRecord, game.homeRecord), so nothing here is invented; the .v2-when line stays. To keep the team record from reading like a capper record, it moved out of the column heads and now sits under the full team name in the matchup header ("Dallas Cowboys / 1-1"), well away from the capper rows and beside a full club name rather than a three-letter abbreviation. That also shortens the column heads to "DAL" plus the count chip, so the chip no longer risks wrapping. The Over/Under heads keep their juice (-110, from the fixture total line) under a separate .v2-px class so it is never styled as a record. The "no price, graded at -110" chip now sits on its own full-width line (.v2-pl) and breaks once, deliberately, after "no price," so it never splits mid-phrase in the narrow column. The stat line dropped to 11.5px with a tighter gap so record, money, and ROI fit on one line in the ~113px body on most rows. The mirrored chevron moved 2px inward with a 16px gutter so it clears the center divider with margin. Everything else is unchanged.
designs.free_tier_notes: Free tier keeps the whole scoreboard: matchup header, both column heads with their counts, the slot count lines, the total band, and every row's pick, price chip, record, money, ROI, source badge, and recorded time. Only the capper name cell is redacted, one per row, rendered as a muted blurred-text placeholder inside .v2-name (a short block in --surface2 with a --border ring, no real characters), and the initials disc shows a neutral dot instead of letters. Rows stay tappable but route to the subscribe sheet. One subscribe prompt, a single line in --accent beneath the count line, reads "Subscribe to see who these cappers are." The counts, the humility line, the unqualified line, and the grading note stay exactly as shown. No blur wall, no dimmed columns, no hidden slots.
designs.graded_state_notes: After the game finalizes the layout does not move. The matchup header gets the final score under each team name where the record now sits (score in --text at 14px 700, record moved to muted small type next to it), and the .v2-when line reads "Final". Each row's pick line gets a small result chip after the price: W in --green, L in --red, Push in --muted, using the same .v2-chip shape. The slot count lines in the column heads do not change (counts are counts) and no side is marked as having "won". Money and ROI on each row stay the capper's NFL season figures, not the single-game result, so the numbers a reader tapped through pregame are the same numbers after. The total band shows the final total next to 44.5 in muted type. The humility line, the unqualified line, and the grading note are unchanged.

issues: Game header content is not in the fixture provided to me: "Sun 1:00 PM ET · Soldier Field" and the team records "1-1" (DAL and CHI) are not derivable from the nine-capper fixture. The rule says use fixture content only, invent nothing. If the orchestrator's full fixture carries kickoff time, venue, and team records, this clears; otherwise drop the .v2-when line and the .v2-rec spans on the team heads (the ML -125/+105, spread -1.5/+1.5 (-110), and total 44.5 -110 are all derivable from the capper picks and prices and are fine).

Minor: the team record "1-1" sits in the same muted W-L style as the capper records directly below it; on a fast read it can be mistaken for a capper record. Not a rule violation, but worth a small label or a different treatment if it stays.
layout_risks: Two-column split inside the 338px card interior yields ~163px per column; after the 28px avatar, 8px gap, and 14px chevron gutter the row body is ~113px wide, so nearly every row wraps its stat line (record, money, ROI) and its meta line (source badge + recorded time) onto two lines. All wrap safely via flex-wrap, but rows run tall and the page gets long.

The price chip "no price, graded at -110" (10px) is wider than the ~113px body and has no nowrap, so it breaks mid-phrase inside the chip on Mattcanter, stevet81, and thirdstring. Consider allowing the chip to sit on its own line or shortening the phrase.

Names KnightDasCapital, RiverCityRick, HomeRunHazard, OldSchool0909 at 13px/600 are close to or over the ~113px body width and will ellipsize; truncation is wired correctly (nowrap + overflow hidden + min-width:0 on the flex chain) so it degrades cleanly.
Column head "DAL 1-1 [3 cappers]" is ~155px in a 163px column; with the auto-margin chip it may wrap the chip onto a second line, right-aligned. Cosmetic, flex-wrap handles it.

Mirrored right column uses row-reverse plus right-aligned text with the chevron on the left edge; equal weight is preserved, but right-aligned ellipsis on names and a left-pointing chevron may feel unusual on a tap target. Check on device that the left-edge chevron does not collide with the center divider (::before at left:50%, which lands in the 12px gap, so it should clear).
critique.design_notes: The mirrored two-column Sides layout is a genuinely distinct direction and reads as fair by construction: identical 1fr columns, a hairline center divider, matching count chips, and a separate Total band with its own Over/Under split. Visual quality is disciplined (token-only colors, tabular numerals, initials discs, chevron affordance with hover/active/focus states), but the 163px columns are dense on a 390px phone and most rows wrap to four or five lines, so it trades scanability for symmetry; the free-tier state is not rendered and should redact one name cell per row with a single subscribe prompt while counts stay visible.
